questions.stem: The scores of ten pupils in a short Mathematics test are $3, 5, 3, 4, 5, 3, 4, 3, 5, 4$. In a frequency table of this data, what is the frequency of the score $3$?
questions.explanation: A tally of the list shows that $3$ appears four times (the 1st, 3rd, 6th and 8th scores). The frequency of a value is simply how many times it occurs, so the frequency of $3$ is $4$.

distractorRationale.a: This is the frequency of $4$ (or of $5$), not of $3$
distractorRationale.c: This is the score itself, or a miscount of the tallies
distractorRationale.d: This is the total number of scores, $\sum f$, not the frequency of one value

questions.stem: In a class of $40$ students, $10$ chose football as their favourite sport. If a pie chart of the choices is drawn, the angle of the football sector is
questions.explanation: The pie-chart angle is $\frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total}} \times 360^\circ = \frac{10}{40} \times 360^\circ = 90^\circ$. One quarter of the class chose football, so the sector is a right angle.

distractorRationale.a: Used the frequency as the angle, without scaling it to $360^\circ$
distractorRationale.b: Took $10\%$ of $360^\circ$, treating the $10$ students as a percentage of $100$ rather than of $40$
distractorRationale.d: Halved $90^\circ$, or used $\frac{10}{80} \times 360^\circ$

questions.stem: The Mathematics scores of twelve SS1 students are $5, 7, 8, 6, 7, 9, 5, 8, 6, 7, 4, 9$. How many students scored $7$ or more? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: The scores of $7$ or more are $7, 8, 7, 9, 8, 7, 9$ — seven values. The remaining five scores ($5, 6, 5, 6, 4$) are all less than $7$. Building a frequency table first makes this count reliable.

questions.stem: A pie chart of $90$ traders at Mile 12 market uses a sector of $80^\circ$ for those who sell yam. How many of the traders sell yam?
questions.explanation: The frequency is $\frac{\text{angle}}{360^\circ} \times \text{total} = \frac{80}{360} \times 90 = 20$. So $20$ of the $90$ traders sell yam.

distractorRationale.a: Divided $80$ by $10$, without using the $360^\circ$ full turn
distractorRationale.b: Used $\frac{80}{360} \times 72$ or halved $80$ then adjusted incorrectly
distractorRationale.d: Took the angle itself as the number of traders

questions.stem: Grouped test scores are recorded in the classes $0$–$9$, $10$–$19$ and $20$–$29$. The class boundaries of the class $10$–$19$ are
questions.explanation: For discrete data grouped in classes such as $10$–$19$, the true class boundaries sit halfway to the next class. That places the lower boundary at $9.5$ and the upper boundary at $19.5$, so the histogram bars touch with no gaps.

distractorRationale.a: These are the class limits, not the class boundaries
distractorRationale.c: Moved half a unit the wrong way, inward from each limit
distractorRationale.d: Jumped a whole unit instead of half a unit

questions.stem: A histogram is drawn for classes of unequal width. The class $10$–$15$ has frequency $10$. The frequency density of this class is
questions.explanation: Frequency density is frequency divided by class width. The class $10$–$15$ has width $5$, so the density is $\frac{10}{5} = 2$. Histogram bar height must be frequency density whenever the class widths are not equal, otherwise the areas would misrepresent the frequencies.

distractorRationale.b: Gave the class width instead of dividing frequency by width
distractorRationale.c: Used the frequency as the bar height, which is only correct for equal-width classes
distractorRationale.d: Divided width by frequency instead of frequency by width

questions.stem: The marks of $80$ students are shown on a cumulative frequency curve. The lower quartile is the mark that corresponds to a cumulative frequency of
questions.explanation: On an ogive, $Q_1$ is read at a cumulative frequency of $\frac{n}{4}$. Here $n = 80$, so $\frac{80}{4} = 20$. Go across from $20$ on the cumulative-frequency axis to the curve, then down to the mark axis.

distractorRationale.b: This is the median position, $\frac{n}{2}$, not $Q_1$
distractorRationale.c: This is the upper-quartile position, $\frac{3n}{4}$
distractorRationale.d: This is the total number of students, used for $Q_4$ which is not a quartile

questions.stem: A cumulative frequency curve is drawn for the scores of $200$ candidates in a JAMB mock. The upper quartile $Q_3$ is the score corresponding to a cumulative frequency of
questions.explanation: The upper quartile is read at cumulative frequency $\frac{3n}{4}$. For $n = 200$ that is $\frac{3 \times 200}{4} = 150$. The median would be at $100$ and $Q_1$ at $50$.

distractorRationale.a: This is the $Q_1$ position, $\frac{n}{4}$
distractorRationale.d: This is the total number of candidates, not a quartile position
